memoryText: But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Amos 5:24 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is the climax of God’s message through Amos. It comes right after God says that he hates their feasts, despises their assemblies, and will not listen to their songs. What he wants in place of all that is this.

“But let justice roll down like waters.” The image is of a flood. The Hebrew word for “roll down” suggests a torrent of water in a wadi, pouring through a dry land. It is not a trickle or a drip. The picture is of justice as something abundant, powerful, and unstoppable.

“Justice” is about fairness, the setting right of wrongs. It means that the poor are not trampled, that the weak are protected, that courts are honest, and that the powerful are held accountable.

“And righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.” Righteousness is the character that produces justice: faithfulness to God and to others. The stream is “ever-flowing,” like a perennial spring that does not dry up in summer. Righteousness is not an occasional burst but a constant supply.

In a land where many streams dried up each summer, the image of an ever-flowing stream would have been especially welcome. God wants a justice that does not fail.

How does this verse apply to us? It does not tell us to stop worshiping. It tells us that worship and justice belong together. Our songs and prayers must flow into our workplaces, our families, and our communities.

For the Christian, the source of this stream is Christ. He is the righteous one, who brings justice to the nations (Isaiah 42:1-4). And his Spirit is the living water that flows from within his people (John 7:38). Ask him to make you a channel of justice.
weekInReview: This week you followed the divided kingdom into the age of the writing prophets. You read the paradox of Jeroboam II’s prosperity, and the collapse of the northern kingdom that came after. You read the psalms of Asaph and of David that warn against empty religion and boasting in evil. And you spent the end of the week with Amos, the shepherd from Tekoa who announced judgment on the nations and then on Israel, because those who had been given much had trampled the poor. You heard God say that he hates their feasts and wants justice to roll down like waters. And you ended with the promise that God will rebuild David’s fallen shelter. The week taught that privilege brings responsibility, that worship without justice is an offense, and that God keeps his promise of restoration.
reflectionQuestions: God says through Amos that he hates empty worship. What would make your worship more real this week, in your heart and in how you live?

Amos 9:11-12 promises the rebuilding of David’s fallen tent, and Acts 15 says this is fulfilled in Christ and the church. How does this change how you see the church, and the nations who are part of it?
Who are the “poor and needy” in your life, and what does it mean for justice to roll down toward them?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to let justice roll down like waters.
Thank him for rebuilding David’s fallen tent in Christ.
Ask him to make you a channel of his justice.
